units.title: Unit 1: The Relational Model
units.description: Relations, schemas, keys, integrity constraints, and null values.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a *candidate key*?
options: Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies every tuple in a relation
A minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies every tuple
The single attribute designated to represent the primary identifier
Any attribute that appears as a foreign key in another relation
questions.explanation: A superkey uniquely identifies tuples; a candidate key is a **minimal** superkey — removing any one attribute from it would break uniqueness.

questions.question: The entity integrity constraint requires that:
options: All attribute values fall within their declared domain
Every non-null foreign key value matches a primary key in the referenced relation
No attribute of a primary key may hold a null value
No two tuples may share the same value for any single attribute
questions.explanation: Entity integrity ensures every tuple is definitively and uniquely identifiable via its primary key.

questions.question: Referential integrity is violated when:
options: A primary key attribute contains a null value
A non-null foreign key value has no matching primary key value in the referenced relation
Two tuples have the same non-key attribute value
An attribute value falls outside its declared domain
questions.explanation: Correct answer: B

questions.question: A primary key attribute may contain NULL values.
questions.explanation: Entity integrity requires every primary key attribute to be non-null.

questions.question: A ___ key in one relation references a primary key in another relation.
questions.explanation: A foreign key stores values that reference a key in another relation.

units.title: Unit 2: SQL: Defining and Modifying Data
units.description: SQL DDL and DML: creating, changing, inserting, updating, and deleting data.

questions.question: Which SQL statement removes both the stored data *and* the schema of a table?
options: `DELETE FROM Student;`
`TRUNCATE TABLE Student;`
`DROP TABLE Student;`
`ALTER TABLE Student REMOVE ALL;`
questions.explanation: `DELETE FROM` removes rows but leaves the schema intact. `DROP TABLE` removes both the schema and all data.

questions.question: The `ON DELETE CASCADE` referential action means:
options: Deleting a referenced tuple sets the foreign key column to null
Deleting a referenced tuple raises an error and is blocked
Deleting a referenced tuple automatically deletes all referencing tuples
Deleting a referenced tuple replaces the foreign key with a default value
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C

questions.question: Which constraint ensures that a *non-primary-key* column accepts only distinct (non-duplicate) values?
options: `NOT NULL`
`CHECK`
`UNIQUE`
`DEFAULT`
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C

questions.question: `DELETE FROM Student` removes rows but keeps the table schema.
questions.explanation: `DELETE FROM` removes data. `DROP TABLE` removes both data and schema.

questions.question: The referential action `ON DELETE ___` automatically deletes referencing rows when the referenced row is deleted.
questions.explanation: `ON DELETE CASCADE` propagates deletion from the referenced row to dependent rows.

units.title: Unit 3: SQL: Querying Data
units.description: SQL querying with filtering, grouping, joins, subqueries, and null handling.

questions.question: Which clause is used to filter the *results of groups* in a `GROUP BY` query?
options: `WHERE`
`HAVING`
`FILTER`
`ON`
questions.explanation: `WHERE` filters individual rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation and can reference aggregate functions.

questions.question: What does `SELECT DISTINCT CourseNo FROM Enrol` return?
options: The first occurrence of each CourseNo value in storage order
All CourseNo values sorted alphabetically
Each unique CourseNo value, with duplicate occurrences removed
Only CourseNo values that appear more than once
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C

questions.question: What is the difference between `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(Grade)` when applied to a table with 10 rows, 3 of which have a null Grade?
options: Both return 10
`COUNT(*)` returns 10; `COUNT(Grade)` returns 7
Both return 7
`COUNT(*)` returns 7; `COUNT(Grade)` returns 10
questions.explanation: `COUNT(*)` counts every row regardless of nulls. `COUNT(attr)` counts only rows where that attribute is non-null.

questions.question: `WHERE` filters individual rows before grouping, while `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation.
questions.explanation: `WHERE` is applied before grouping; `HAVING` is applied after groups and aggregates are formed.

questions.question: The SQL clause used to filter grouped query results is ___.
questions.explanation: `HAVING` filters groups after `GROUP BY` and can use aggregate expressions such as `AVG(...)`.

units.title: Unit 4: Conceptual Database Design (ER/EER)
units.description: Conceptual database design using ER and EER modelling.

questions.question: A *weak entity type* is best defined as:
options: An entity with no attributes of its own
An entity that cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes alone and depends on an owner entity
An entity that participates only partially in a relationship
An entity involved in a recursive (self-referencing) relationship
questions.explanation: A weak entity has a partial key but needs the primary key of its owner to form a complete identifier.

questions.question: In an ER diagram, **double lines** connecting an entity type to a relationship type indicate:
options: A M:N cardinality ratio
A derived attribute
Total participation — every entity instance must participate in the relationship
A recursive relationship
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C

questions.question: Which cardinality ratio describes: "each employee works for *at most one* department, and each department may have *many* employees"?
options: M:N
1:N (one department, many employees)
M:1 (many employees, one department)
questions.explanation: Answer note: (equivalently C, depending on direction convention — the key constraint is many employees to one department)

questions.question: A weak entity can be uniquely identified using only its own attributes.
questions.explanation: A weak entity depends on an owner entity; its identifier combines the owner key with its partial key.

questions.question: In ER modelling, double lines indicate ___ participation.
questions.explanation: Double lines indicate total participation in an ER relationship.

units.title: Unit 5: Functional Dependencies and Keys
units.description: Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, closures, candidate keys, and minimal covers.

questions.question: A functional dependency X → Y is **trivial** if:
options: X is a superkey of the relation
Y ⊆ X (Y is a subset of X)
X and Y are disjoint attribute sets
Y is a prime attribute
questions.explanation: A trivial FD holds in every relation because Y is already contained within X — e.g., {A, B} → A is always satisfied.

questions.question: Given FDs A → B and B → C, which Armstrong's axiom derives A → C?
options: Reflexivity
Augmentation
Transitivity
Union
questions.explanation: Correct answer: C

questions.question: The *closure* X⁺ of a set of attributes X under a set of FDs F is:
options: The set of all FDs logically implied by F
The set of all attributes that X functionally determines using F
The set of all superkeys that contain X
The minimal cover of F restricted to X
questions.explanation: Correct answer: B

questions.question: A functional dependency X -> Y is trivial when Y is a subset of X.
questions.explanation: Trivial dependencies always hold because the right-hand side is already included in the left-hand side.

questions.question: If X+ contains every attribute of relation R, then X is a ___.
questions.explanation: When the closure of X includes all attributes, X functionally determines the whole tuple, so X is a superkey.

units.title: Unit 6: Normalisation
units.description: Normal forms, decomposition, lossless joins, and dependency preservation.

questions.question: A relation violates **2NF** if:
options: It contains an attribute with a non-atomic (multi-valued) domain
A non-prime attribute is functionally dependent on only part of a composite candidate key
A non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key through another non-prime attribute
A determinant of a non-trivial FD is not a superkey
questions.explanation: (Option A describes a 1NF violation; option C describes a 3NF violation; option D describes a BCNF violation.)

questions.question: **BCNF** requires that for every non-trivial FD X → A in R:
options: Either A is a prime attribute, or X is a superkey
X is a superkey
X contains the primary key as a subset
A is not a prime attribute
questions.explanation: 3NF allows the "A is a prime attribute" escape clause; BCNF does not — the only permissible case is X being a superkey.

questions.question: Which statement is true of **3NF** but **NOT** of BCNF?
options: All partial dependencies on candidate keys are eliminated
A decomposition into this normal form always preserves all functional dependencies
Every determinant of any non-trivial FD is a superkey
A lossless-join decomposition into this form is always achievable
questions.explanation: 3NF synthesis guarantees both lossless join and dependency preservation. BCNF decomposition guarantees lossless join but not necessarily dependency preservation.

questions.question: BCNF decomposition always preserves all functional dependencies.
questions.explanation: BCNF decomposition guarantees lossless join, but it may lose dependency preservation.

questions.question: A lossless-join decomposition reconstructs the original relation without introducing ___ tuples.
questions.hint: Unwanted extra rows from a join
questions.explanation: Lossless join means the decomposed relations join back to exactly the original relation, with no spurious tuples.

units.title: Unit 7: Relational Algebra
units.description: Relational algebra operators, equivalences, and SQL translation.

questions.question: The selection operation σ_φ(R) returns:
options: A subset of the *attributes* of R satisfying condition φ
All tuples of R that satisfy condition φ, with the same schema as R
Each distinct value of the attribute named in φ
All combinations of tuples from R and another relation satisfying φ
questions.explanation: Selection filters rows; the result has the same schema as the input relation.

questions.question: In set-based (formal) relational algebra, why does projection π always produce a relation without duplicate tuples?
options: Projection automatically sorts the output by the projected attributes
Relations are defined as sets, so all RA results are sets — duplicates are eliminated by definition
Projection includes a built-in DISTINCT clause
Tuples with duplicate projected values are replaced by null
questions.explanation: In formal RA, every expression returns a relation (a set of tuples). SQL uses bag semantics and requires explicit DISTINCT.

questions.question: If relation R has 4 tuples and relation S has 3 tuples and they share **no** attributes, the Cartesian product R × S has:
options: 7 tuples
At most 4 tuples
12 tuples
A number equal to the overlapping values between R and S
questions.explanation: Cartesian product: |R × S| = |R| × |S| = 4 × 3 = 12.

questions.question: Selection chooses rows, while projection chooses columns.
questions.explanation: Selection (sigma) filters tuples; projection (pi) keeps selected attributes.

questions.question: In formal relational algebra, projection eliminates duplicates because relations are ___.
questions.explanation: Formal relational algebra uses set semantics, so duplicate tuples are removed by definition.
